passage: Transcript, kitchen meeting, the Grey Heron restaurant, Tuesday after close. Chef Marchand: Autumn menu, decisions tonight, the printer needs it Friday. The duck stays, obviously. The argument is the fish course. Sous-chef Ito: The mackerel dish died in August. We sold four all month. It is a beautiful dish and nobody orders it, and there is no shame in admitting the room has voted. Marchand: The room is wrong. Ito: The room pays us. Marchand: What replaces it? Ito: The smoked eel from the Fennmarsh smokehouse, with the beetroot three ways we trialed at the staff dinner. Eleven of twelve staff picked it blind over the mackerel. Pastry chef Okonjo: I was the twelfth, and I abstained because I do not eat fish, so it was eleven of eleven, which is worse for the mackerel. Marchand: The eel costs double. Ito: And plates at 4 dollars more with a better margin by my sheet, which is on the board. The smokehouse can supply forty portions a week, guaranteed, and the story is local, which the mackerel, whatever its virtues, was not; it came up on the truck from the city market like everything we pretend it does not. Marchand: You have been rehearsing this speech. Ito: Since August, chef. Marchand: The eel goes on. The mackerel gets one farewell weekend, priced honestly, and I will cook every one myself. Also decided tonight, since we are being brave: the cheese trolley returns, Okonjo's chestnut dessert replaces the parfait, and the bread charge, which I have hated for two years, is abolished; bread is a greeting, not a transaction. Print deadline Friday, Ito does the final costings tomorrow. Family meal in ten minutes; it is the eel, naturally.
question: How many portions a week can the smokehouse guarantee?

passage: Minutes, verbatim, Corrievale Search and Rescue, debrief of the Beckon Ridge callout, training officer presiding. Officer Strand: Standard debrief rules: timeline first, no blame language, lessons written down. Timeline. Team Leader Voss: Call from police at 15:40, walker overdue, last seen at the ridge cairn at noon. Team of eight assembled at the Garrow Bridge trailhead by 16:25, which is our best assembly this year. Two search pairs up by 16:40, sweep line on the east shoulder by 17:15. Subject located 18:52 by pair two, Okafor and Reyes, in the boulder field 300 meters below the cairn, off the path, ankle fracture, conscious, cold. Strand: The find, how? Okafor: Honestly? The whistle. We stopped for the hourly listening halt, per the new protocol, and heard three blasts, faint, downwind. Without the scheduled stop we walk past that boulder field on the path side and hear nothing over our own boots. Strand: Note one, then: the listening halts found this casualty. They cost us twenty minutes across the search and they found the casualty. That goes in the training plan in bold. Extraction? Voss: Splint, casualty bag, wheeled stretcher to the trailhead by 20:30, ambulance transfer 20:45. One equipment note: the stretcher's third wheel bearing seized on the scree, and we carried the last 400 meters. The bearing was on the maintenance list from the June exercise and did not get done. Strand: Note two, and this one has no soft phrasing: a known fault on the list since June reached a live callout. The gear officer and I will rebuild the maintenance tracking this month, and the stretcher does not deploy again until signed off. Anything for the subject's file? Reyes: She did everything right: told someone her route, stayed put once hurt, whistled at intervals. The casualty is why this debrief is short. Strand: So minuted. Debrief closed, 21:40.
question: At what time was the subject located?

passage: Transcript, planning session, Odd Volumes Book Festival, six weeks out. Director Plum: Headline problem first: the marquee. The supplier we have used for nine years went into liquidation on Friday. Options, Verity. Operations, Verity Marsh: Two real ones. Fennick Events can supply the same size, 400 seats, at 6,200 dollars, which is 1,700 over the old price, and they want the booking by Wednesday. Or the town offers the drill hall free, capacity 280, if we thank the council from every stage, which costs nothing and is worth exactly what it costs. Plum: The Saltway reading sold 380 last year. We cannot put 380 people in a 280 hall. Marsh: We split the big events across two sessions in the hall, afternoon and evening. The authors' agent says her client would actually prefer two smaller rooms, the marquee echo was in her notes from last year, underlined. Treasurer Gupta: The 1,700 saved is our entire schools program margin. I will fight for the hall on numbers alone. Plum: And rain? The marquee held the courtyard crowd every year. The hall has a roof by definition. I have talked myself into it. Decision: drill hall, split sessions, council thanked warmly and often, and Fennick told promptly and kindly, since we may need them next year. Marsh: The signage all says courtyard. Plum: Reprint the signage; Gupta, find the 300 dollars, you just saved 1,700. Next item: the poet who will not travel by train.
question: What is the drill hall's capacity?

passage: Verbatim minutes, Brindmoor Golf Club greens committee, the rabbit question, chair recording attendance at eleven, apologies two. Chair Osgood: The rabbits. Head Greenkeeper Fry, the report. Fry: Population up threefold by the dawn counts, the seventh fairway is a lacework, and on Tuesday a member, whom I will not name because he has suffered enough, put his ankle in a burrow on the eleventh and his ball, I am told, in the pond. Damage to greens themselves: minor still, they prefer the fairway rootzone, but the third green's collar shows scraping as of this week. Osgood: Options and costs. Fry: Fencing the boundary with the warren common: 11,000 dollars for rabbit mesh at the correct depth, which is two feet buried, and anything shallower is a rabbit amusement. Ferreting, licensed, over winter: 1,800 a season, effective for a season, then they return; it is mowing, not surgery. Or the long answer: the boundary hedge restored thick at the base, which is where we lost it when the flail contract replaced the laying, plus the mesh on the worst two hundred meters only, 4,200 all in, and the hedge does the rest in three years. Member Trask: Three years is a long lacework. Fry: The mesh handles the worst now; the hedge retires the problem. Cheap, slow, and permanent, or dear, fast, and annual. Golf clubs usually buy the second one, if the committee will forgive me. Osgood: The committee forgives the accuracy. Motion: the hedge and partial mesh plan at 4,200, ferreting this winter only as a bridge at 1,800, fencing quote declined, review in twelve months. Moved Trask, seconded Bell. Carried six to one, the dissent recorded as wanting the full fence and the dissenter's ankle recorded as the one in question. Laughter, and the chair rules the minute stands.
question: How much does the hedge and partial mesh plan cost all in?

passage: Transcript, parish hall, Little Marden pantomime committee, casting the dame and other storms. Chair Whitlow: Order, please, and I use the word hopefully. First: the dame. Norman has played the dame for nineteen years, and Norman, as we all know, had his hip done in July, and his surgeon, his wife, and finally Norman himself have ruled him out of the ladder scene, and there is no dame without the ladder scene, it is the whole of act two. Norman, from the floor: I could do a modified ladder. Chair Whitlow: Your wife is behind you, Norman. Norman: The dame is retired. Applause. Chair Whitlow: The committee's proposal: Norman directs. The dame passes to young Mr. Okafor from the bakery, who understudied the last two years, fits the frocks with alteration, and, this is the clincher, can actually sing, which will be a novelty for the part. Mrs. Pell: The frocks are Norman's own. Norman: The frocks come with the part, like a bishopric. Sustained applause. Chair Whitlow: Second item, the horse. The costume's rear half was eaten by mice in the pavilion over summer, only the rear, the front is fine. Quotes: a new whole horse, 800 dollars; a rear half made to match by Mrs. Danvers, 90 dollars in materials, if, her condition, she never again has to be inside it. Carried by acclamation before I finished the sentence, thank you. Casting of the rear half is referred to the director. Norman: The director accepts, and has a list. Laughter. Chair Whitlow: Rehearsals Tuesdays and Thursdays from the 14th, hall booked, urn mended, and the fire officer has asked, again, that the pyrotechnic finale remain, and I quote his letter, imaginary. So moved. We are done in record time; the pub is open.
question: How much will Mrs. Danvers charge in materials for the horse's rear half?

passage: Minutes taken in full, Tarnbeck Angling Association, water quality emergency meeting. Chair Ellison: You have all seen the beck. Milky gray from the Fothergill culvert down to the weir since Saturday morning. What we know, from Dr. Musa, who came out on her Sunday, for which the association's thanks. Dr. Musa: Sampled at six points Sunday and again Tuesday. The plume is limestone fines, rock dust, not sewage and not chemical: mineral, inert, but at these concentrations it blankets gravel and smothers eggs, and you have redds below that culvert. The source is upstream of my access, but the particle profile matches quarry washings. Ellison: The Whinstone quarry reopened its washing plant in August. Secretary Boyd: I walked the culvert line Monday. The settlement lagoon at the quarry has a breach in the lower bund, you can see it from the footpath, and the overflow runs to the old field drain, which is the Fothergill culvert's feed. I photographed everything, timestamped. Musa: That matches the profile. For the record, the fish are not dying today; the eggs will die over weeks if the blanketing continues through spawning. There is a window, but it is a window. Ellison: Actions. One: report to the environment agency tonight, with Boyd's photographs and Musa's samples, as a formal pollution incident. Two: a letter to the quarry, copied to the agency, offering a site meeting this week; they may not know, bunds breach quietly. Three: no member speaks to the newspaper until the quarry has had five working days, and I want that minuted as fairness. Boyd: And if they stall? Ellison: Then item three expires on its own schedule and the photographs are very clear. Moved, seconded, carried nine to nil. Musa resamples Friday, association pays the lab fees, 240 dollars from the habitat fund.
question: What did Dr. Musa identify the plume as?

passage: Transcript, staff meeting, Wrenfield Primary School, the nativity logistics session, head teacher presiding. Head Ms. Adeyemi: Twenty minutes, everything decided, that is the tradition. Costumes first. Mrs. Fallon: The angel wings crisis is resolved: the laundrette donated eleven sets of net curtains and Mrs. Ochoa's mother has turned them into wings that, I will say it, are better than the bought ones. Photographs will circulate. Adeyemi: The donkey. Mr. Voss: The donkey head was repaired with the glue gun and a prayer. It will survive one more year, but I want it minuted, for the third year running, that the donkey head is on borrowed time. Adeyemi: Minuted with the same solemnity as always. Casting disputes? Mrs. Fallon: One. Both Hartley twins want to be the star, the celestial one, and refuse to share by alternating nights. Their mother proposes, and I quote her note, two stars, citing precedent that there are many stars in the sky. Adeyemi: Astronomy defeats us. Two stars, stage left and right, and the east star gets one extra line to keep the plot moving. Fallon: The east star line goes to whichever twin is not sulking at dress rehearsal. Adeyemi: A casting principle with wide application. Timings: doors at 2, curtain 2:30, forty minutes running time if the sheep cooperate, which brings me to the sheep. Voss: The reception class sheep number nineteen this year. We have nine costumes. Adeyemi: Then ten children are shepherds, we have crooks in the cupboard from the year of the strike. Final item: Mr. Pemberton retires at Christmas after 34 years, and the last scene will end with the whole school singing his favorite, which the children think is a secret and he thinks is a secret, and both sides are wrong, and it will be perfect. Meeting closed at nineteen minutes; a record stands.
question: How many sheep costumes does the school have?

passage: Verbatim record, Gorsemoor Beekeepers Association, winter meeting, the sugar question and other matters. Chair Innes: First, subscriptions. The treasurer reports 84 paid of 91 members, and the seven stragglers know who they are and one of them is my brother. Laughter. Second, the bulk sugar order. Quartermaster Reyes: The wholesaler quotes 62 cents a kilo for the association order if we clear two tons. Last year we ordered 1.7 tons and scrambled in September. My proposal: two tons, the discount funds the difference, surplus stored at the Grange apiary, dry loft, mouse proofed since the incident. Innes: The incident is now formally part of association vocabulary. Moved? Carried, unanimous, my brother abstaining on grounds of not having paid. Third, the winter losses survey. Secretary Whitcombe: Forms back from 61 members: average losses 9 percent, our best winter in a decade, and the correlation in the returns is plain: members who treated for mite in August lost 6 percent, members who treated in October lost 15. August treatment is the difference, same as the county data says, and our own numbers now say it in our own accent. Innes: That figure goes in the newsletter in large type. Fourth: the association hives at the school. The caretaker reports the observation hive queen failed in November; the spring plan is a nucleus from the Grange stock, and the science coordinator asks that the requeening be done, her words, during lesson time with maximum drama. Reyes: Beekeeping as theater. Innes: All beekeeping is theater, Mr. Reyes, the bees simply decline to rehearse. Spring lecture: Dr. Fenwick on swarm control, hall booked for March 9. Tea rota unchanged. Closed 8:40.
question: What loss rate did members who treated for mite in August report?

passage: Transcript, harbor users committee, Skellport, the dredging schedule dispute. Chair Marsh: The dredger is booked for the last two weeks of April, and the objection everyone has heard informally is now formal, from the fishing fleet. Skipper Doyle: April is the start of the crab season. Two weeks of dredger in the channel at the season's start, with the plume over the pot grounds off the east wall, costs my boats the best fortnight of the spring. Move it to March. Marina Manager Osei: March fills the visitor berths for the lifting bridge festival; a dredger through the moorings that fortnight cancels bookings we confirmed a year ago, and the marina carries 60 percent of the harbor dues these days, which pays for, among other things, the dredging. Doyle: The fleet carried the dues for eighty years before a single yacht arrived, and the channel silted where it silts because the river does not consult bookings. Chair Marsh: The engineer's constraint, before this becomes historical: the dredger company offered three windows: March, late April, or September. September? Engineer Voss: September works for depths; the survey shows we have margin until October. But September risks the equinox weather, and a weather delay in September pushes into the closed season for disposal at sea, which strands the spoil barge in the harbor for the winter at 400 dollars a day demurrage. Doyle: And the April plume over the pot grounds? Voss: Real but manageable: the silt curtain option adds 6,000 to the contract and keeps the plume inside the channel line. The company confirmed availability this morning. Chair Marsh: So: April with the silt curtain, plume contained, festival untouched, crab grounds screened. Fleet? Doyle: With the curtain in the contract, in writing, the fleet withdraws the objection. Osei: The marina will split the curtain cost with the general fund. Chair Marsh: Then it is settled and minuted: April window, curtain at 6,000 split evenly, and the committee notes with relief that the river remains the only party not negotiating. Carried, nine to nil.
question: How much does the silt curtain option add to the contract?

passage: Minutes in full, Dellwick Camera Club, competition night rules review, following the autumn exhibition. Chair Fenwick: One agenda item, by demand: the phone photograph question. The autumn open was won, as everyone knows, by Mrs. Adler's picture of the heron at the weir, taken, as everyone also knows, on her telephone, and the club has talked of little else since. The complaint, formally lodged by two members, is that phone images should compete in their own class, separate from what the complaint calls proper cameras. Mrs. Adler, you asked to speak first. Adler: Three sentences, as promised. The heron did not ask what I was holding. The judges scored the picture not knowing and ranked it first of ninety-one entries. If the club now builds a fence around the winners' table, it should at least be honest that the fence is for me. Silence, then some applause, the secretary notes. Fenwick: The complainants. Mr. Ostler: It is not about Mrs. Adler, whose picture is excellent. A phone computes its pictures; the sky in that image was blended by software from three exposures before she saw it. My camera records what the lens gives. The classes exist so like competes with like. Judge Emeritus Pryce, invited opinion: Frank has described every camera made in thirty years, including his own, whose sensor and processor conspire behind his back constantly. The line he wants does not exist in the equipment; it exists only in the year a member stopped reading manuals. Judge by the print. It is the only honest wall in photography. Fenwick: Motion arising, from the committee: all images compete together; the entry form adds one line stating capture device, for information and the annual statistics, not for classing; and the winter program adds a phone camera evening, taught, if she will, by Mrs. Adler. Vote: 31 for, 6 against, 2 abstentions. Carried. Mrs. Adler will teach the evening, and Mr. Ostler, the minutes record with pleasure, has signed up for it.
question: Of how many entries was Mrs. Adler's picture ranked first?
